questions.q: The principle of selective photothermolysis depends on confining thermal damage to the target chromophore. For this to occur, the laser pulse duration must be:
opts: Shorter than or equal to the thermal relaxation time (TRT) of the target
Longer than the thermal relaxation time of the target
Equal to the thermal relaxation time of the surrounding dermis
Independent of the target's thermal relaxation time
questions.exp: Selective photothermolysis (Anderson & Parrish, 1983) requires a wavelength absorbed preferentially by the target, sufficient fluence, and a pulse duration shorter than or equal to the target's thermal relaxation time (TRT — time for the target to lose 50% of its heat). This confines heat to the target before it diffuses to surrounding tissue. TRT is proportional to the square of the target diameter.

questions.q: Picosecond lasers are increasingly preferred over Q-switched (nanosecond) lasers for tattoo and pigment removal. The principal mechanism conferring their advantage is:
opts: Higher melanin absorption coefficient due to a longer wavelength output
Deeper dermal penetration allowing treatment of subcutaneous pigment
A dominant photoacoustic (photomechanical) effect from ultrashort pulses fragmenting pigment into smaller particles
Continuous-wave delivery producing sustained bulk heating of the ink
questions.exp: Picosecond pulses (10⁻¹² s) are far shorter than the TRT of tattoo ink particles, so energy is delivered faster than heat can dissipate. This shifts the dominant mechanism from photothermal (nanosecond Q-switched) to photoacoustic/photomechanical — a rapid pressure wave that shatters pigment into much smaller fragments, enabling more efficient macrophage clearance with fewer sessions and less thermal collateral damage.

questions.q: In fractional photothermolysis, the treated columns of thermally affected tissue are termed microthermal treatment zones (MTZs). The principle underlying faster healing compared to fully ablative resurfacing is:
opts: Each MTZ is treated at a lower fluence, preventing any coagulative necrosis
MTZs target only the epidermis, sparing the dermis entirely
The laser operates in continuous-wave mode allowing immediate re-epithelialisation
Intervening zones of spared, viable tissue between MTZs serve as reservoirs for rapid re-epithelialisation
questions.exp: Fractional photothermolysis creates an array of microscopic columns of thermal injury (MTZs) surrounded by untreated viable tissue. These spared 'bridges' of intact epidermis and dermis act as reservoirs of keratinocytes and provide rapid migration for re-epithelialisation — typically within 24–48 hours — versus 1–2 weeks for fully ablative resurfacing, while still stimulating dermal remodelling.

questions.q: The CO₂ laser (10,600nm) is highly effective for ablative resurfacing because its wavelength is strongly absorbed by:
opts: Oxyhaemoglobin in superficial dermal vessels
Intracellular and tissue water
Melanin within epidermal melanocytes
Collagen cross-links in the reticular dermis
questions.exp: The CO₂ laser at 10,600nm is strongly absorbed by tissue water, which is the dominant chromophore in skin. This causes rapid vaporisation of water-containing tissue (ablation) with a thin zone of residual thermal damage that stimulates collagen contraction and remodelling. Er:YAG (2940nm) has an even higher water absorption coefficient, producing more precise ablation with less residual thermal effect.

questions.q: Compared to the CO₂ laser, the Er:YAG laser (2940nm) for skin resurfacing characteristically produces:
opts: More precise ablation with less residual thermal damage and reduced collagen contraction
Deeper penetration with greater haemostasis during ablation
Greater intraoperative bleeding control due to a wider coagulation zone
A higher risk of post-procedure scarring due to deeper thermal injury
questions.exp: Er:YAG (2940nm) is absorbed by water ~12–16× more strongly than CO₂ (10,600nm). Energy is deposited in a very thin tissue layer, producing precise ablation with minimal residual thermal damage. The trade-off: less collagen contraction (less tightening) and poorer haemostasis (more pinpoint bleeding) than CO₂, which has a broader coagulation zone enabling better intraoperative bleeding control.

questions.q: The KTP (potassium-titanyl-phosphate) laser emits at 532nm. This wavelength is generated by:
opts: Pumping an alexandrite rod with a flashlamp at high repetition rate
Stimulated emission from an argon-ion gas medium
Raman shifting of a diode laser through an optical fibre
Frequency-doubling of the 1064nm Nd:YAG beam through a KTP crystal
questions.exp: The KTP laser is a frequency-doubled Nd:YAG: passing the 1064nm beam through a potassium-titanyl-phosphate crystal halves the wavelength to 532nm (and doubles the frequency). At 532nm it is well absorbed by both oxyhaemoglobin and melanin, making it useful for superficial vascular lesions (facial telangiectasia) and epidermal pigmented lesions.

questions.q: Intense pulsed light (IPL) differs fundamentally from laser devices because IPL:
opts: Produces coherent, collimated monochromatic light at a single wavelength
Operates only in the infrared spectrum above 1000nm
Emits non-coherent, polychromatic light over a broad spectrum filtered by cut-off filters
Delivers continuous-wave rather than pulsed energy
questions.exp: IPL is not a laser. It uses a flashlamp to emit non-coherent, polychromatic (broadband, typically 400–1200nm) light. Cut-off filters select the lower wavelength boundary to target specific chromophores (e.g., 560nm for vascular, 640nm for pigment/hair). Because it lacks coherence and monochromaticity, IPL is more versatile but less selective than a laser of a defined wavelength.

questions.q: For laser hair reduction in a Fitzpatrick type II patient with coarse dark hair, the alexandrite laser (755nm) is frequently chosen because at this wavelength:
opts: Water is the dominant chromophore, ablating the follicular bulge
Melanin absorption is high, providing strong selectivity for the pigmented hair shaft and matrix
Oxyhaemoglobin absorption coagulates the perifollicular vasculature preferentially
Deep penetration to 7mm allows targeting of subcutaneous follicles
questions.exp: At 755nm, melanin absorption is high, giving the alexandrite laser strong selectivity for the melanin-rich hair shaft, matrix, and bulge. This makes it very effective in lighter skin (Fitzpatrick I–III) with dark hair. In darker skin (IV–VI), high epidermal melanin absorption raises the risk of epidermal injury, so the longer-wavelength 1064nm Nd:YAG (lower melanin absorption) is safer.

questions.q: The long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser (1064nm) is the safest laser for hair reduction in Fitzpatrick skin types V–VI primarily because at 1064nm:
opts: Melanin absorption is comparatively low, sparing epidermal melanin while still targeting follicular melanin at depth
Water absorption is maximal, vaporising the follicle directly
The wavelength is too short to penetrate beyond the epidermis
It selectively heats oxyhaemoglobin rather than melanin
questions.exp: At 1064nm, melanin absorption is relatively low compared to shorter wavelengths (e.g., 755nm alexandrite, 694nm ruby). This reduces unwanted absorption by the heavily melanised epidermis of dark skin while still depositing enough energy in the follicular melanin at depth (1064nm penetrates deeply). Combined with epidermal cooling, this makes Nd:YAG the safest choice in skin types V–VI.

questions.q: During pulsed dye laser (PDL, 595nm) treatment of facial telangiectasia, immediate post-treatment purpura (bruising) indicates that the fluence/pulse settings caused:
opts: Selective melanin destruction in the overlying epidermis
Subthreshold heating insufficient to affect the vessel
Rapid intravascular coagulation and rupture of the targeted vessel (purpuric threshold reached)
Direct ablation of the stratum corneum
questions.exp: Purpura after PDL signifies that the purpuric threshold was reached: rapid heating coagulates intravascular oxyhaemoglobin and ruptures the vessel wall, extravasating blood. While historically associated with maximal efficacy, modern 'sub-purpuric' protocols use longer pulse durations and lower fluences to achieve clearance with less downtime, particularly for diffuse erythema and rosacea.

questions.q: Glycolic acid is the most widely used alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA) for superficial peeling. Its keratolytic potency relative to other AHAs is greatest because:
opts: It is lipophilic and concentrates within sebaceous follicles
It has the smallest molecular weight of the AHAs, allowing the deepest and fastest epidermal penetration
It self-neutralises on contact with skin, preventing over-penetration
It chelates calcium in desmosomes irreversibly
questions.exp: Glycolic acid (MW 76 Da) is the smallest AHA, conferring the fastest and deepest penetration and the strongest keratolytic effect at equivalent concentrations. It reduces corneocyte cohesion by interfering with desmosomal/ionic bonding in the lower stratum corneum. Crucially, glycolic acid does NOT self-neutralise — it must be neutralised (with sodium bicarbonate or water) at the desired endpoint to prevent uncontrolled penetration and injury.

questions.q: Salicylic acid is classified as a beta-hydroxy acid peel. The property that makes it especially suitable for comedonal/oily acne-prone skin is that it is:
opts: Hydrophilic, so it remains in the aqueous epidermis without entering follicles
A strong dermal collagen stimulant reaching the reticular dermis
Only active above pH 5, limiting it to very superficial peeling
Lipophilic, allowing penetration into sebum-filled follicles, with self-neutralising pseudofrosting
questions.exp: Salicylic acid is lipophilic, enabling it to penetrate sebaceous, sebum-rich follicles — making it ideal for comedonal and inflammatory acne. It is comedolytic and anti-inflammatory. As it dries, it precipitates as a white 'pseudofrost' (crystallised salicylic acid, not protein coagulation), which is self-limiting and signals the endpoint — reducing the risk of over-penetration, an advantage in darker skin.

questions.q: Jessner's solution is a classic combination superficial peel. Its three active components are:
opts: Resorcinol, salicylic acid, and lactic acid in ethanol
Glycolic acid, kojic acid, and hydroquinone in propylene glycol
Trichloroacetic acid, phenol, and croton oil in water
Salicylic acid, mandelic acid, and citric acid in ethanol
questions.exp: Classic (Combes') Jessner's solution contains resorcinol 14g, salicylic acid 14g, and lactic acid (85%) 14g, made up to 100mL with ethanol. It produces superficial peeling via keratolysis and is often used to 'prime' the skin before a TCA peel. Modified Jessner's formulations replace resorcinol (an allergen/toxicity concern) with citric acid or lactic acid.

questions.q: During a phenol–croton oil (Baker-Gordon) deep peel, the single most important systemic intraoperative monitoring requirement is:
opts: Continuous blood pressure monitoring for hypertensive crisis
Hourly serum potassium measurement for hyperkalaemia
Continuous cardiac (ECG) monitoring because phenol is cardiotoxic and can cause arrhythmias
Pulse oximetry alone, as phenol primarily causes hypoxaemia
questions.exp: Phenol is absorbed systemically and is cardiotoxic — it can precipitate atrial/ventricular arrhythmias (tachycardia, PVCs, bigeminy, fibrillation). Continuous ECG monitoring is mandatory, peels are applied cosmetic-unit by unit with timed intervals (e.g., 15 minutes per unit), and IV hydration is given to promote renal/hepatic clearance. Phenol is also hepatotoxic and nephrotoxic, so it is avoided in patients with cardiac, hepatic, or renal disease.

questions.q: Unlike glycolic acid, trichloroacetic acid (TCA) does not require active neutralisation at the endpoint because TCA:
opts: Is buffered to physiological pH within the formulation
Causes protein coagulation (frosting) and is self-neutralising once it has reacted with tissue keratin
Penetrates too slowly to ever reach a dangerous depth
Is rapidly metabolised by epidermal esterases on contact
questions.exp: TCA works by precipitating/coagulating epidermal and dermal proteins (keratin coagulation), producing the characteristic white 'frost'. Once it has reacted with tissue proteins it is effectively self-neutralising — there is no need to wash it off to stop the reaction (though dilution with water/cool compresses improves comfort). Depth is judged by frost level rather than by timed neutralisation as with AHAs.

questions.q: Mandelic acid is sometimes preferred over glycolic acid for superficial peeling in darker (Fitzpatrick IV–VI) skin because mandelic acid:
opts: Has a much lower pKa, making it far more aggressive
Is lipophobic and cannot penetrate the epidermis at all
Is a beta-hydroxy acid with intrinsic antibacterial coating
Has a larger molecular weight, producing slower, more uniform penetration and a lower risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
questions.exp: Mandelic acid (MW 152 Da) is roughly twice the size of glycolic acid (76 Da). Its larger molecule penetrates the stratum corneum more slowly and evenly, producing gentler, more controlled exfoliation. This reduces irritation and the risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, making it well suited to darker skin and to acne (it also has mild antibacterial properties).

questions.q: Topical retinoids (tretinoin) improve photoaged skin and acne. Their primary molecular mechanism is binding to:
opts: Nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RAR), modulating gene transcription of keratinocyte differentiation and collagen genes
Membrane G-protein-coupled receptors triggering cAMP elevation
Cytoplasmic tyrosinase, directly blocking melanin synthesis
Toll-like receptor 2 on sebocytes, reducing sebum output
questions.exp: Tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid) binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RAR-α, -β, -γ), which heterodimerise with retinoid X receptors (RXR) and modulate transcription of genes governing keratinocyte proliferation/differentiation, comedolysis, and collagen synthesis (upregulating procollagen, downregulating MMPs). This explains both anti-acne (normalised follicular keratinisation) and anti-ageing (dermal collagen) effects.

questions.q: Hydroquinone remains a benchmark depigmenting agent. Long-term, high-concentration use carries the risk of exogenous ochronosis, which is characterised by:
opts: Permanent depigmentation due to total melanocyte destruction
Paradoxical blue-black pigmentation from accumulation of ochronotic (homogentisic acid–like) pigment in the dermis
Diffuse erythema from telangiectasia formation
Atrophy and striae from transepidermal collagen loss
questions.exp: Hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase, reducing melanin synthesis. Prolonged use of high concentrations (especially in darker skin and with sun exposure) can cause exogenous ochronosis — paradoxical blue-black/grey-brown hyperpigmentation from deposition of an ochronotic pigment (yellow-brown banana-shaped fibres) in the papillary dermis. It is difficult to treat; prevention via limited duration, sun protection, and ≤2–4% concentrations is key.

questions.q: The original Kligman's formula for melasma is a triple-combination topical. Its three active ingredients are:
opts: Kojic acid, azelaic acid, and ascorbic acid
Hydroquinone, tretinoin, and a topical corticosteroid (e.g., dexamethasone)
Glycolic acid, salicylic acid, and niacinamide
Arbutin, tranexamic acid, and hydrocortisone
questions.exp: Kligman & Willis' formula combines hydroquinone (tyrosinase inhibition), tretinoin (enhances epidermal turnover/penetration and reduces HQ oxidation), and a topical corticosteroid (reduces irritation and melanocyte metabolism). The modified Kligman's (e.g., hydroquinone 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone 0.01%) is the most evidence-supported topical for moderate-to-severe melasma.

questions.q: Azelaic acid is a useful agent in acne and pigmentation. Its mechanism on pigmentation differs from hydroquinone in that azelaic acid:
opts: Irreversibly destroys mature melanocytes regardless of activity
Acts only as a physical UV blocker reducing melanogenesis
Increases melanosome transfer to keratinocytes, redistributing pigment
Selectively inhibits abnormally hyperactive melanocytes (a competitive, reversible tyrosinase inhibitor) while sparing normal ones
questions.exp: Azelaic acid is a competitive, reversible inhibitor of tyrosinase and is selectively cytotoxic/antiproliferative toward hyperactive and abnormal melanocytes, with little effect on normally pigmented skin — so it is useful for melasma and PIH with low risk of hypopigmentation. It also has antibacterial (against C. acnes) and anti-keratinising properties, explaining its dual role in acne and rosacea.

questions.q: Kojic acid, derived from Aspergillus fermentation, achieves skin lightening principally by:
opts: Chelating copper at the active site of tyrosinase, inhibiting the enzyme
Blocking the transfer of melanosomes to keratinocytes via PAR-2
Accelerating epidermal turnover to shed pigmented corneocytes
Reducing dermal melanin via direct macrophage stimulation
questions.exp: Kojic acid inhibits tyrosinase by chelating the copper ions essential to the enzyme's catalytic active site (tyrosinase is a copper-dependent oxidase). This blocks the rate-limiting conversion of tyrosine to DOPA and DOPA to dopaquinone. It is often combined with other agents (e.g., arbutin, glycolic acid) but can be a contact sensitiser with prolonged use.

questions.q: Niacinamide (nicotinamide) reduces hyperpigmentation through a mechanism distinct from tyrosinase inhibitors. It principally:
opts: Chelates copper in tyrosinase like kojic acid
Acts as a sunscreen absorbing UVB at 305nm
Inhibits the transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to surrounding keratinocytes
Destroys melanocyte dendrites permanently
questions.exp: Niacinamide does not inhibit tyrosinase or melanin synthesis directly; instead it inhibits the transfer of mature melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes (reducing pigment deposition in the epidermis by 35–68% in studies). It also improves the skin barrier (increasing ceramide synthesis), reduces sebum, and has anti-inflammatory effects — making it a versatile, well-tolerated cosmeceutical.

questions.q: Oral tranexamic acid is used for refractory melasma. Its mechanism for reducing pigmentation is:
opts: Direct copper chelation at the tyrosinase active site
Competitive antagonism of melanocortin-1 receptor
Selective destruction of dermal melanophages
Inhibition of plasmin, reducing UV-induced plasminogen activation and downstream prostaglandin/arachidonic-acid–driven melanogenesis
questions.exp: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic (lysine analogue) that inhibits plasminogen-to-plasmin conversion. In skin, UV-induced keratinocyte plasmin generation raises arachidonic acid and α-MSH, stimulating melanocytes; TXA interrupts this keratinocyte–melanocyte signalling and also reduces melasma-associated neovascularisation. Low-dose oral TXA (e.g., 250mg BD) shows good efficacy, though thromboembolic risk must be screened.

questions.q: Arbutin is a popular natural skin-lightening agent. Chemically and mechanistically, arbutin is best described as:
opts: An ascorbic acid ester that reduces existing melanin by antioxidant action
A naturally occurring glycosylated derivative of hydroquinone that inhibits tyrosinase, releasing hydroquinone gradually
A retinoid analogue acting on nuclear RAR receptors
A copper-independent inhibitor of DOPA-oxidase only
questions.exp: Arbutin (hydroquinone-β-D-glucopyranoside) is a glycosylated hydroquinone derivative found in bearberry and other plants. It inhibits tyrosinase and tyrosinase-related protein activity, and slowly releases hydroquinone, providing a gentler, more sustained depigmenting effect with less irritation than free hydroquinone. Alpha-arbutin is more stable and potent than beta-arbutin.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin is one of the most potent biological toxins. In cosmetic practice, one 'unit' of onabotulinumtoxinA is defined as:
opts: The amount equal to the median lethal dose (LD50) when injected intraperitoneally into a defined strain of mice
One nanogram of purified neurotoxin protein per vial
The dose producing 50% chemodenervation of the human frontalis muscle
A fixed molar quantity of the 150-kDa neurotoxin core
questions.exp: A unit of botulinum toxin is a biological potency measure — defined as one mouse LD50 (the dose lethal to 50% of a tested group of mice when injected intraperitoneally). Crucially, units are NOT interchangeable between products because the assay differs: roughly 2.5–3 Dysport (abobotulinumtoxinA) units approximate 1 Botox (onabotulinumtoxinA) unit. This is why doses must be product-specific.

questions.q: When converting between botulinum toxin brands, the commonly cited approximate dose ratio between abobotulinumtoxinA (Dysport) and onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) is:
opts: 1 : 1 (interchangeable unit for unit)
1 : 4 (Dysport four times more potent per unit)
10 : 1 (Botox ten times more potent per unit)
Approximately 2.5–3 : 1 (Dysport units to Botox units)
questions.exp: Because potency assays differ between manufacturers, units are not interchangeable. The most widely used conversion is approximately 2.5–3 units of Dysport (abobotulinumtoxinA) per 1 unit of Botox (onabotulinumtoxinA). IncobotulinumtoxinA (Xeomin) is roughly 1:1 with Botox. Misapplying a 1:1 ratio between Botox and Dysport leads to significant under- or over-dosing.

questions.q: After cosmetic botulinum toxin injection to the glabellar complex, the typical onset and peak duration of clinical effect are approximately:
opts: Onset within minutes; peak effect at 24 hours; duration 2 weeks
Onset in 2–3 days; visible effect by 1–2 weeks; clinical effect lasting ~3–4 months
Onset at 3 weeks; peak at 8 weeks; permanent effect thereafter
Onset immediately; effect lasting 12 months from a single session
questions.exp: Botulinum toxin A acts by cleaving SNAP-25, preventing acetylcholine vesicle fusion. Clinical onset begins around 2–3 days, with peak effect by 1–2 weeks. The effect on dynamic rhytides typically lasts about 3–4 months, after which axonal sprouting and SNAP-25 turnover restore neuromuscular transmission, necessitating repeat treatment.

questions.q: Eyelid ptosis is a feared complication of glabellar botulinum toxin treatment. It results from inadvertent diffusion of toxin to the:
opts: Orbicularis oculi, causing the lower lid to droop
Frontalis, causing brow elevation failure only
Levator palpebrae superioris, weakening upper eyelid elevation
Corrugator supercilii, producing medial brow descent
questions.exp: True eyelid (upper lid) ptosis follows toxin diffusion through the orbital septum to the levator palpebrae superioris, which elevates the upper eyelid. It typically appears 1–2 weeks post-injection. Prevention: inject ≥1cm above the orbital rim, avoid excessive volume/units, and instruct the patient not to rub or lie down immediately. Apraclonidine 0.5% drops (α-agonist stimulating Müller's muscle) can provide temporary lift.

questions.q: The glabellar frown is produced mainly by the corrugator supercilii and which other muscle, both targeted in cosmetic botulinum toxin treatment of frown lines?
opts: Frontalis (which elevates the brow)
Orbicularis oris (which purses the lips)
Procerus (which produces the horizontal nasal-root crease)
Zygomaticus major (which elevates the angle of the mouth)
questions.exp: The glabellar complex comprises the corrugator supercilii (draws brows medially, producing vertical frown lines), the procerus (depresses the medial brow, producing the horizontal crease at the nasal root), and depressor supercilii/medial orbicularis fibres. Standard glabellar treatment injects the corrugators and procerus (classic 5-point pattern). The frontalis elevates the brow and is treated separately for horizontal forehead lines.

questions.q: An injector wishes to minimise unwanted spread of botulinum toxin to adjacent muscles. Which factor MOST increases the field of diffusion?
opts: Using a smaller-gauge (finer) needle
Higher reconstitution volume (greater dilution) and higher injected volume per site
Injecting more superficially into the dermis
Using incobotulinumtoxinA rather than onabotulinumtoxinA
questions.exp: Diffusion (field of effect/'halo') increases with higher reconstitution volume and larger injected volume per point — a more dilute, larger bolus spreads further through tissue planes. To limit spread to neighbouring muscles, injectors use smaller volumes of more concentrated toxin and precise placement. Dose (units) and injection technique also matter; needle gauge has minimal effect on diffusion.

questions.q: Hyaluronic acid (HA) dermal fillers vary in their rheological property G′ (elastic modulus). A filler with a HIGH G′ is best suited for:
opts: Fine superficial lines and lip vermilion border definition
Deep structural support and projection (e.g., cheekbone, chin, nasal dorsum augmentation)
Subdermal skin-quality 'bioremodelling' over wide areas
Tear-trough correction requiring maximal softness
questions.exp: G′ (elastic modulus) reflects a gel's firmness/resistance to deformation. High-G′ fillers resist compression and provide strong lift and projection, ideal for deep structural support over bone (cheekbones, chin, jawline, nose). Low-G′, softer fillers are chosen for delicate superficial areas (lips, fine lines, tear troughs) where a firm gel would feel lumpy or visible. Matching rheology to anatomical site is key to natural results.

questions.q: The most catastrophic complication of dermal filler injection is vascular occlusion leading to skin necrosis or blindness. The anatomical region carrying the HIGHEST risk of blindness is the:
opts: Nasolabial fold via the facial artery
Lateral cheek via the transverse facial artery
Lip body via the inferior labial artery
Glabella/nasal dorsum, via retrograde embolisation through the supratrochlear/dorsal nasal arteries to the ophthalmic/central retinal artery
questions.exp: The glabella, nasal dorsum, and forehead are highest-risk for blindness because their vessels (supratrochlear, supraorbital, dorsal nasal arteries) anastomose with the ophthalmic artery. Inadvertent intra-arterial injection under pressure can drive filler retrograde into the ophthalmic and central retinal artery, causing sudden, often irreversible vision loss. Prevention: aspirate, inject slowly with low pressure, use cannulas, and inject small aliquots while moving.

questions.q: If vascular occlusion from HA filler is suspected (blanching, livedo, severe pain), the immediate definitive antidote is high-dose:
opts: Hyaluronidase injected into and around the affected area to dissolve the occluding HA
Intralesional triamcinolone to reduce inflammation
Subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin only
Topical nitroglycerin paste as sole therapy
questions.exp: Hyaluronidase is the antidote for HA-filler vascular occlusion. High doses (often hundreds of units, repeated, flooding the affected vascular territory — not just the injection point) are given urgently to enzymatically degrade the obstructing HA and restore perfusion. Adjuncts include warm compresses, massage, topical nitroglycerin, and aspirin. Time is critical — irreversible necrosis/visual loss occurs within hours, so a hyaluronidase protocol must always be on hand.

questions.q: Calcium hydroxylapatite (CaHA, Radiesse) differs from hyaluronic acid fillers because, in addition to immediate volumising, CaHA:
opts: Is rapidly reversible with hyaluronidase if a complication occurs
Provides only a temporary effect lasting under 4 weeks
Stimulates neocollagenesis as fibroblasts deposit collagen around the CaHA microspheres (biostimulation)
Is composed of cross-linked sugar polymers identical to native dermis
questions.exp: CaHA consists of calcium hydroxylapatite microspheres suspended in a carboxymethylcellulose gel carrier. The gel gives immediate volume; as it resorbs, the microspheres act as a scaffold stimulating fibroblasts to lay down new collagen (biostimulation), so the effect is longer-lasting (~12–18 months). Importantly, CaHA is NOT reversible with hyaluronidase — a key safety consideration in high-risk vascular areas.

questions.q: Poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA, Sculptra) is classified as a collagen biostimulator rather than a true filler because it:
opts: Provides immediate, fully visible volume correction at the time of injection
Works gradually over weeks–months by inducing a subclinical inflammatory/foreign-body response that drives fibroblast collagen synthesis
Is degraded within 48 hours leaving no lasting effect
Must be reversed with hyaluronidase if overcorrection occurs
questions.exp: PLLA microparticles induce a controlled subclinical inflammatory/foreign-body response, stimulating fibroblasts to produce new collagen gradually over weeks to months. The initial post-injection volume (from the diluent) subsides within days; true correction develops slowly and is built up over multiple sessions. Adequate dilution, deep injection, and vigorous post-treatment massage reduce the risk of delayed nodules/granulomas. It is not reversible with hyaluronidase.

questions.q: A patient develops a bluish discolouration over the tear trough several weeks after HA filler. This Tyndall effect occurs because:
opts: The filler triggered methaemoglobinaemia in overlying skin
A vascular occlusion caused deoxygenated venous pooling
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation deposited dermal melanin
Light scattering by superficially placed (too shallow) HA gel preferentially reflects blue wavelengths
questions.exp: The Tyndall effect is an optical phenomenon: when HA filler is placed too superficially in thin skin (classically the tear trough), the translucent gel scatters shorter (blue) wavelengths of light more than longer ones, giving a bluish hue. Prevention: inject deep (supraperiosteal/sub-orbicularis), use small volumes of low-G′ filler, and avoid overcorrection. Treatment: hyaluronidase to dissolve the superficial gel.

questions.q: Finasteride is widely used for androgenetic alopecia. It reduces scalp dihydrotestosterone by selectively inhibiting:
opts: Type 2 (and to a lesser extent type 1) 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme converting testosterone to DHT
Aromatase, blocking conversion of testosterone to oestradiol
The androgen receptor directly within the dermal papilla
17-alpha-hydroxylase in the adrenal cortex
questions.exp: Finasteride is a competitive inhibitor of 5-alpha-reductase type 2 (the predominant isoenzyme in the hair follicle dermal papilla and prostate), with weaker activity at type 1. By blocking testosterone→DHT conversion it lowers scalp and serum DHT (~60–70%), the key androgen driving follicular miniaturisation in genetically susceptible follicles. It does not block the androgen receptor or inhibit aromatase.

questions.q: Dutasteride is sometimes used (off-label) for androgenetic alopecia in finasteride non-responders because, unlike finasteride, dutasteride:
opts: Blocks the androgen receptor in addition to 5-alpha-reductase
Has no effect on serum DHT and acts only locally
Inhibits BOTH type 1 and type 2 5-alpha-reductase isoenzymes, producing greater DHT suppression
Stimulates new follicle neogenesis directly via Wnt signalling
questions.exp: Dutasteride is a dual inhibitor of 5-alpha-reductase types 1 and 2, whereas finasteride mainly inhibits type 2. This dual blockade suppresses serum DHT more profoundly (>90% vs ~70%), and type 1 is relevant in sebaceous glands and skin. Greater efficacy comes with a longer half-life and a similar but potentially greater sexual side-effect profile; it is not a direct androgen-receptor blocker.

questions.q: Topical minoxidil is a prodrug. Its conversion to the active form, and hence variable clinical response between patients, depends on the scalp enzyme:
opts: 5-alpha-reductase type 1 converting minoxidil to dihydrominoxidil
Sulfotransferase SULT1A1, which sulphates minoxidil to minoxidil sulphate (the active metabolite)
Catechol-O-methyltransferase methylating minoxidil
Cytochrome P450 3A4 hydroxylating minoxidil
questions.exp: Minoxidil is a prodrug requiring sulfation by sulfotransferase SULT1A1 in the outer root sheath to form minoxidil sulphate, the active moiety that opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels. Inter-individual variation in scalp SULT1A1 activity explains why ~30–40% of users respond poorly (low-sulfotransferase phenotype). Sulfotransferase assays are being explored to predict responders, and oral minoxidil bypasses some of this limitation.

questions.q: Beyond requiring sulfation, the active metabolite minoxidil sulphate promotes hair growth principally by:
opts: Blocking dihydrotestosterone at the androgen receptor
Directly inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase in the dermal papilla
Competitively antagonising prostaglandin D2 receptors on follicles
Opening ATP-sensitive potassium channels, causing vasodilation and shortening telogen while prolonging anagen
questions.exp: Minoxidil sulphate opens ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channels in vascular smooth muscle and follicular cells, producing vasodilation and increased perifollicular blood flow, and — more importantly — it shortens telogen, prematurely triggers anagen, and prolongs the anagen growth phase, increasing follicle size. It has no effect on androgens or 5-alpha-reductase, which is why it is often combined with finasteride for additive benefit.

questions.q: The Hamilton-Norwood classification is used to grade which condition, and a Norwood Grade VII represents:
opts: Male androgenetic alopecia; the most advanced stage with only a sparse band of hair around the sides and back
Female pattern hair loss; complete frontal hairline loss
Alopecia areata severity; total scalp involvement (alopecia totalis)
Scarring alopecia extent; full cicatricial replacement
questions.exp: The Hamilton-Norwood scale grades male androgenetic alopecia from I (no significant recession) to VII (most severe). Grade VII denotes extensive loss leaving only a narrow horseshoe-shaped band of hair over the temples and occiput, with a sparse, fine donor zone. The scale guides prognosis and hair-transplant donor planning. Female pattern hair loss is graded by the Ludwig (or Sinclair) scale instead.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman develops diffuse hair shedding 3 months after a high fever and childbirth. The scalp is non-scarred and the hair-pull test is positive with telogen (club) hairs. The characteristic latency between the trigger and shedding in telogen effluvium is:
opts: Immediate, within 24–48 hours of the insult
1 week, coinciding with the acute illness
Approximately 2–4 months, as affected anagen follicles are shifted prematurely into telogen and then shed
1–2 years after the precipitating event
questions.exp: In acute telogen effluvium, a systemic stressor (fever, childbirth, surgery, crash diet, drugs) precipitates a synchronised premature shift of anagen follicles into telogen. Because telogen lasts ~3 months before the club hair is shed, diffuse shedding becomes apparent roughly 2–4 months after the trigger. It is self-limiting once the trigger resolves, with full regrowth, unlike anagen effluvium (days–weeks, e.g., chemotherapy).

questions.q: On trichoscopy (dermoscopy of the scalp), which finding is characteristic of alopecia areata?
opts: Peripilar brown halo and hair-diameter diversity
White cicatricial patches with loss of follicular ostia
Comma and corkscrew hairs
Exclamation-mark hairs, yellow dots, black dots, and short vellus regrowth
questions.exp: Alopecia areata trichoscopy classically shows exclamation-mark hairs (tapered proximally), yellow dots (keratin/sebum-filled follicular openings), black dots (cadaverised hairs), broken hairs, and short tapered regrowing vellus hairs. Peripilar halo and hair-diameter diversity suggest androgenetic alopecia; loss of follicular ostia indicates scarring alopecia; comma/corkscrew hairs indicate tinea capitis.

questions.q: Comparing the two main hair-transplant harvesting techniques, follicular unit excision (FUE) differs from the strip method (FUT) chiefly in that FUE:
opts: Always yields a higher total graft count from the donor area
Leaves a linear donor scar requiring sutured closure
Extracts individual follicular units via small punches, leaving tiny dot scars and no linear scar
Permits microscopic dissection of grafts under direct vision from a removed strip
questions.exp: FUE harvests individual follicular units directly from the donor scalp using small (0.8–1.0mm) punches, leaving multiple tiny circular ('dot') scars and no linear scar — allowing short haircuts and faster recovery. FUT (strip) removes a strip of donor scalp that is microscopically dissected into grafts, leaving a single linear scar. FUT can yield more grafts per session with high follicle survival but leaves a visible linear scar.

questions.q: Maximising graft survival in hair transplantation depends on minimising 'out-of-body' time and ischaemic injury. The most important measures during graft storage are:
opts: Storing grafts dry at room temperature to prevent maceration
Warming grafts to 37°C to maintain metabolic activity
Keeping grafts hydrated in chilled (~4°C) holding solution to reduce ischaemic metabolic demand, and minimising time out of the body
Soaking grafts in 70% ethanol to prevent bacterial contamination
questions.exp: Follicular grafts are vulnerable to desiccation and ischaemia-reperfusion injury. Survival is optimised by keeping grafts continuously moist in a chilled (~4°C) holding/storage solution (saline, lactated Ringer's, or specialised hypothermic media such as HypoThermosol/ATP-containing solutions), which lowers metabolic demand, and by minimising the duration grafts spend outside the body. Dry storage, warming, or alcohol exposure damages follicles.

questions.q: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) for hair restoration and skin rejuvenation works by delivering concentrated growth factors. The growth factors released from platelet alpha-granules that drive this effect include:
opts: PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF, EGF, and IGF-1, which stimulate angiogenesis, fibroblast activity, and follicular stem cells
Tumour necrosis factor-alpha and interleukin-1 as the primary regenerative signals
Histamine and serotonin promoting vasodilation only
Erythropoietin and thrombopoietin stimulating marrow precursors
questions.exp: PRP concentrates platelets 3–5× above baseline; on activation, alpha-granules release PDGF, TGF-β1, VEGF, EGF, IGF-1, FGF, and others. These promote angiogenesis, fibroblast proliferation/collagen synthesis, and stimulate dermal papilla cells and follicular bulge stem cells (prolonging anagen) — underpinning use in androgenetic alopecia and skin rejuvenation. TNF-α and IL-1 are pro-inflammatory, not the regenerative mediators of PRP.

questions.q: Low-level laser (light) therapy (LLLT) devices for hair growth (e.g., 650nm laser combs/caps) are proposed to work through photobiomodulation. The principal molecular target is:
opts: Melanin in the hair shaft, which is selectively heated to stimulate the matrix
Water in follicular cells, producing a micro-thermal ablative effect
Haemoglobin, increasing perifollicular oxygen delivery by coagulation
Cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) in mitochondria, boosting ATP production and modulating reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide
questions.exp: LLLT/photobiomodulation uses red/near-infrared light (~630–680nm) at low fluences that do not heat or ablate tissue. The primary photoacceptor is cytochrome c oxidase (mitochondrial complex IV); light absorption displaces inhibitory nitric oxide, increasing electron transport, ATP synthesis, and modulating reactive oxygen species and signalling. In follicles this is thought to shift telogen follicles into anagen and prolong the growth phase.

questions.q: Cryolipolysis ('fat freezing') for non-invasive body contouring reduces localised fat by:
opts: Immediate mechanical rupture of adipocyte membranes by ice-crystal formation during the treatment
Triggering cold-induced apoptosis of adipocytes, which are selectively sensitive to cooling, with gradual clearance over weeks
Thermal coagulation of subcutaneous fat at temperatures above 45°C
Ultrasonic cavitation forming gas bubbles that lyse fat cells
questions.exp: Cryolipolysis exploits the greater sensitivity of lipid-rich adipocytes (versus surrounding water-rich tissue) to cold injury. Controlled cooling (~ −5 to −10°C at the applicator) induces adipocyte apoptosis without damaging skin, nerves, or vessels. Apoptotic adipocytes are gradually cleared by macrophages over 1–3 months, yielding a ~20–25% reduction in the treated fat-layer thickness. A rare delayed complication is paradoxical adipose hyperplasia.

questions.q: Deoxycholic acid (ATX-101 / Kybella) is an FDA-approved injectable for submental fat reduction. Its mechanism of fat reduction is:
opts: Cold-induced crystallisation of intracellular lipids
Inhibition of lipogenesis via PPAR-gamma antagonism
Detergent-like adipocytolysis — disrupting adipocyte cell membranes, causing cell lysis followed by a local inflammatory clearance response
Selective photothermolysis of adipocyte chromophores
questions.exp: Deoxycholic acid is a naturally occurring bile acid that acts as a detergent: injected into subcutaneous fat, it physically disrupts adipocyte cell membranes, causing adipocytolysis (cell lysis). The released lipids and cellular debris trigger a local macrophage-mediated inflammatory response and tissue remodelling over weeks. It is non-selective, so careful injection technique (avoiding the marginal mandibular nerve and dermis) is essential to prevent nerve injury and skin necrosis.

questions.q: High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) achieves non-surgical facial lifting by delivering focused thermal energy to a specific, consistent depth. The target tissue plane that distinguishes HIFU from most radiofrequency devices is the:
opts: Stratum corneum and upper epidermis
Papillary dermis just beneath the basement membrane
Subcutaneous fat lobules only
Superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) at ~4.5mm, the plane addressed in surgical facelifts
questions.exp: HIFU focuses ultrasound to create discrete thermal coagulation points at precise, controllable depths — notably ~4.5mm to reach the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), the fibromuscular layer tightened in surgical facelifts, as well as ~3.0mm (deep dermis) and ~1.5mm. This deep, focused heating induces collagen contraction and neocollagenesis for lifting. Most RF devices heat the dermis more diffusely and do not selectively target the SMAS at a fixed focal depth.
